interactionPlan.concept: Filtering in the frequency domain is a pointwise multiplication of an image's spectrum by the filter's transfer function, selectively scaling spatial frequencies.
learningObjectives: After engaging with this figure, the student will understand that spatial filtering (convolution) is mathematically equivalent to pointwise multiplication in the Fourier domain.
The student will be able to explain how a transfer function acts as a frequency-by-frequency scale factor (or 'volume knob') for image features.
The student will be able to predict the visual effects on an image when specific spatial frequencies (low, high, or directional) are filtered out.
interactionPlan.keyInsight: Fourier-domain filtering cannot generate new frequencies; it can only scale, suppress, or preserve the spatial patterns already present in the input image.

interactions.label: Filter Type
interactions.effect: Changes the shape and active region of the 2D transfer function H[u,v], altering which spatial frequencies are allowed to pass through.
interactions.teaches: How different filters target distinct visual structures: low-pass preserves slow variations (smooth regions), high-pass preserves rapid transitions (edges), and directional filters block specific orientations.

interactions.label: Filter Radius
interactions.effect: Dynamically scales the size of the passband or stopband in the 2D transfer function visualization and immediately updates the resulting output spectrum and reconstructed spatial image.
interactions.teaches: The direct relationship between the frequency cutoff boundary in the Fourier domain and the level of detail, blur, or sharpness in the spatial domain.

interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: The interface should reconstruct the flow of the textbook block diagram but populate it with live, visual data: (1) An input image alongside its 2D Fourier Magnitude Spectrum L_in[u,v] (using a log-scaled grayscale/viridis intensity plot). (2) An interactive 2D Transfer Function H[u,v] block (showing a black-and-white mask corresponding to the selected filter type and radius). (3) The output magnitude spectrum L_out[u,v], computed as the pointwise product of L_in and H, alongside the final reconstructed spatial image via Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT). Standard mathematical equations should overlay the arrows to connect the visual flow directly to the algebraic expression: L_out[u,v] = H[u,v] * L_in[u,v].
